toc.title: What I thought I was seeing
What happened with my own client
Why it didn't happen all at once
What they all have in common

blocks.p: I'm a therapist, and I was wrong about trauma recovery. When I first learned the Polyvagal Theory and began understanding the somatic pieces of trauma work, I got something wrong. I thought recovering from trauma was done all at once. Here's where I got it wrong, and what I ended up learning.

blocks.h: What I thought I was seeing

blocks.p: I had been learning from Porges' lectures and reading his books and articles, and I was also learning from Peter Levine, his books and the YouTube videos he's published. And I saw things that looked pretty darn miraculous.

You may have heard Levine's story of Nancy, especially if you've read Waking the Tiger, but it comes up a lot. Nancy was heavily traumatized, and in a session with her, for the first time, he recognized that she had some stuck flight energy, some stuck trauma. He gave her the image of a tiger chasing her, and that prompted her to do this shaking, trembling, trauma-releasing type of thing. The idea is that it released the stuck trauma within her.

Then there's a video of Ray, where they're up on stage and Peter Levine is doing some trauma-releasing work with him based on his Somatic Experiencing. Ray has a twitch that he developed from his stuck trauma, and Levine asks him to open his jaw slowly, and it seems like the trauma just gets released.

Someone also sent me access to some of his course videos, I think. In one of them, Levine is working with an infant who had some trauma. He simply, or seemingly simply, put his hand on the baby's back. The baby tensed up, then released, and I think cried it out. Basically, the trauma was released by Peter Levine putting his hand on its back.

All of these seemed like miracles, just incredible trauma-releasing moments. And it's very good trauma work, as best I can tell. I think Levine does some amazing things, and I'm glad he shares a lot of what he does. If I ever went back to some sort of schooling, I would probably seek out a Somatic Experiencing practitioner credential.

He's doing really good work. But as it turns out, Nancy continued to work on her trauma. It wasn't a one-time thing. I didn't note where I got this, but I think it was in one of his books that he says he doesn't really work with clients like that anymore, and that he took more time to slowly ease into the trauma, as best I remember it. I don't think he regretted doing that with her, but it sounds like something he took more time with.

And Ray, the soldier on stage who slowly opens his jaw and releases his trauma? That wasn't a one-time thing either. They had done some preliminary Somatic Experiencing work before getting up on stage, and they had some follow-up meetings as well. His stuck state didn't go away all at once either.

blocks.h: What happened with my own client

blocks.p: So I incorrectly thought my therapy clients were supposed to go through this full-body trauma releasing, shaking and trembling. I thought it was all or nothing. If we could just get unstuck, if we could just discharge all this trauma all at once, that would cure them, right?

But for the most part, I was not seeing that in my clients. The first time I did see the shaking and trembling, I had done something very similar: I had given the client an image. For her, it was running to her grandmother's house, which was a safe place for her. In the image, she was able to visualize running, which allowed some stuck flight and freeze energy to discharge.

Okay, great. And I thought, "This is going to be a miracle. She's going to come back and tell me her life has fundamentally changed, that she's no longer traumatized, that she's succeeding in every domain, in every facet of life."

She came back the next week, and yes, things were kind of different. I remember her telling me she had a stronger emotional baseline, or less of that freeze kind of energy. But for the most part, she was still living in a traumatized state. She was still very much stuck. It wasn't a one-time thing.

So what was happening? Why weren't these people, and my client, able to just access their safety state? Why weren't they just releasing their trauma? Why did the presenting problems we were working on persist?
I'll be honest: I was disappointed in myself. I was frustrated, I was confused, and I was doubting myself as a therapist on this new somatic track.

blocks.h: Why it didn't happen all at once

blocks.p: The reality is there are plenty of reasons why they didn't have a miraculous change:

ul: The present-day family context. Maybe they're lacking co-regulation and they're constantly being re-traumatized.
The path of trauma they went through. Maybe it wasn't the shock trauma variety, but more of a chronic disruption of connectedness.
Not enough distress tolerance built up. We need more distress tolerance, a stronger vagal brake, before releasing trauma.

blocks.p: By the way, that releasing trauma thing doesn't apply to all kinds of trauma. It's more of a shock trauma thing, and I think Peter Levine is known for specializing in shock trauma. That's when someone goes through a thing, or multiple things, where that flight and fight energy gets frozen into their system. They access the mixed state of freeze, where immobilization locks in the flight and fight state. That's shock trauma, the acute life threat reaction, and that's the Peter Levine variety of releasing it.

For the individual who exists in a defensive state more because of a chronic disruption of connectedness, maybe with a very dominant shutdown state, releasing the trauma doesn't exactly apply. For them, it's more about coming out of that dissociative shutdown, out of numbness, into aggression, into power, into their fight state. It's allowing that sympathetic energy to return, not discharging it.

But recovering from either of these paths of trauma, the acute threat reaction or the chronic disruption of connectedness, is not done all at once. I have not found that to be the case, and I haven't met the person who got unstuck from trauma all at once. Maybe it's you. I don't know. I haven't met that person yet. Releasing a shock trauma is not just about shaking and trembling, and allowing sympathetic energy to return is not just about willing it to do so.

blocks.h: What they all have in common

blocks.p: There are many reasons why someone may stay stuck in a defensive state. But the similarity between all these different traumatized people, or bodies, or nervous systems, is that they all have an inability or difficulty accessing their safety state. The very definition of trauma is that there's an inability or difficulty with accessing, or maintaining access to, the safety state.
So developing the vagal brake is necessary for all of us, but in trauma work it's extremely important.
Developing the vagal brake is not a linear process. It's not A to B, or A to Z. It's a very gradual process.

That means there are going to be obstacles along the way. They could be real-life external obstacles, like literal safety problems, or a lack of co-regulation in your home that keeps feeding into and reinforcing that stuck defensive state. There could also be internal world obstacles, like a chronic illness. That's going to put some bumps in the road in your process of building your vagal brake.

But I'm more concerned about the obstacles that emerge from your emotions, your cognitions, your impulses, and your sensations. As you gain more access to your safety state, the stuck state begins to emerge, and [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) climbing happens. You'll go from shutdown up into your fight state. The immobilization of freeze will start to thaw, and then the flight and fight energy may start to emerge. As you make progress in developing your safety state, stuff will come up that your vagal brake may not have the strength to tolerate quite yet.

Basically, the natural process of self-regulation begins to happen. For example, as someone becomes more grounded in the present moment, maybe through using their senses, their shutdown state will naturally alleviate, and fight energy will enter the system. This can be really uncomfortable for people. It's experienced not as power, but as uncomfortable anger. So they go right back down into their shutdown state, unable to really embrace and feel that much mobilization.

There are going to be moments that feel like progress and moments that feel like setbacks. I know it's frustrating, but that is the normal process of change in general. When it comes to developing your safety state, you'll feel steps forward, and along the way you'll probably feel like you're taking some steps back as well.

So trauma is not solved, released, discharged, or relieved all at once. You'll have moments of stepping forward, where the stuck, traumatized state is not dominating your day-to-day existence. And you'll have moments where it's creeping up on you, or leaking out, or maybe even exploding. We don't want that to happen. Ideally, we want the safety state strong enough to handle it so the explosion doesn't happen. But there might be moments of that as well.
Change requires dedication, and it requires practice. You probably already know that. Making change is gradual, and that definitely includes developing the strength of your vagal brake.

I recommend you have some sort of dedicated practice. Maybe it's mindfulness or meditation, or an Instagram guru you follow. Be careful with them, by the way. I was one of them. I'm not there anymore, but be careful with them. If there's something in place that you can dedicate yourself to on a regular basis to help you work on your trauma, I think that's great.

With my therapy clients, we're able to access safety pretty much every session. I can work with them to get there through co-regulation and somatic techniques. Then we can stretch the capacity of their vagal brake by working on their defensive state and then coming back to safety. I always give them some homework to do between sessions. That's part of the dedication and the practice: coming in to therapy, whether it's weekly or biweekly, and also the stuff in between, to keep building the strength of the vagal brake so you can work more directly on the trauma once it's ready.

Building the safety pathways is the primary concern. I do challenge my clients to feel further into their defensive state as they're ready for it. But at the beginning stages, for the most part, we're not doing that. It's a bit much. It's too much. So I work with them on building the safety pathways. You have to do that.

Maybe you're in therapy, or maybe you're doing your own self-regulation, mindfulness, meditation, or unstucking practice. Therapy is different. But what I want you to take from this is that, either way, the point is dedicated practice. In therapy, that's weekly sessions with homework. In your own self-regulation practice, maybe it's a daily fifteen-minute thing. Set up a routine you can rely on, and set yourself on that path to build your vagal brake strength, so that you can eventually work more directly on your stuck state.
It's not an all or nothing thing, this trauma stuff. It's not released all at once, as best I can tell.

The image I have in my mind is an army marching forward. The army is the strength of your safety state, the progress of your safety state. Hopefully that front line is bolstered and strong enough to hold the line as you move forward and work more directly on the stuck defensive state: actually experiencing it on a sensation level, an impulse level, an emotional level, or even a cognitive one. Or even delving into the trauma narrative, if that's what you're working on.
The safety state holds that front line and slowly moves forward into the stuck defensive state, not all at once. Here's how that looks in practice:

ol: Move a little way into the stuck defensive state, and notice what you're capable of.

When you notice some dysregulation coming up, the front line stops. You hold the line, and you replant yourself firmly in your safety state, as much as you can. Make sure the line is refortified with everything it needs.
Once you're reanchored and well regulated, keep marching forward into the stuck defensive state.

blocks.p: Going down the ladder purposefully and mindfully, and then coming right back up and reanchoring in safety, is what builds the strength of those safety pathways.

That's how I'd sum this up: it's not all at once. I was wrong when I was learning this stuff, and I don't want you to make the same mistake and expect a one-time, trauma-releasing home run. So I really invite you to be as patient with yourself as you can.

Change will happen. If you're using some sort of practice, whether it's building safety anchors or something else, and you're moving forward intentionally and not pushing yourself too far, I believe change is very much possible. As you build your safety state, the defensive stuff should ease up more and more, especially if you're not delving into it before you're ready. So have that dedicated practice in place, whatever it is, and really do it. I'd encourage you to focus more on the safety state than on the trauma narrative or the stuck defensive state, until you're ready for it.

When you see those little wins, when you notice your front line marching forward, celebrate it. Notice it. Give yourself a little praise or encouragement, whatever helps you notice it. Maybe it's just closing your eyes for a moment and feeling what success feels like. Give yourself that, please.
And when you have setbacks, notice those too, but learn from them. Rededicate yourself to your practice, keep anchoring in safety, hold that front line, and when you're ready, keep marching forward.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.
